topic: إنقاذ معابد أبو سمبل من مياه بحيرة ناصر

facts: Abu Simbel is in Nubia in southern Egypt.
Ramesses II had the Great Temple cut into living rock.
Four seated colossal figures dominate the Great Temple facade; one was damaged in antiquity.
The nearby Small Temple is associated with Queen Nefertari.
The Great Temple admits sunlight into the inner sanctuary twice a year; do not claim royal birthdays or exact dates.
The temples were moved due to inundation risk linked to the Aswan High Dam; relocation was completed in 1968.
The rising reservoir threatened the temples.
The rescue engineering operation began in 1964.
Specialists from different countries cooperated under UNESCO coordination.
The rock-cut site was carefully divided into blocks, dismantled, moved and reassembled.
The source describes the new location as 65 metres higher and 200 metres inland. Treat both as approximate rounded figures, using حوالي or نحو.
Egypt and Sudan asked UNESCO to help protect Nubian heritage.
A wider Nubian monuments campaign launched in 1960.
Engineers, archaeologists, architects and other experts worked together.
Blocks were numbered and documented before reassembly.
An artificial rocky hill was constructed around the reassembled temples.
The relocated Abu Simbel temples were inaugurated in September 1968.
The rescue helped develop international heritage protection and the World Heritage Convention.
This is a story about conserving heritage alongside modern development, not rejecting the dam.

numeric_policy.note: UNESCO pages use different rounded relocation distances (65/200 versus 64/180); this episode attributes approximate 65/200 to the UNESCO cultural-heritage overview, not exact surveying data.
